posts.title: What's the most important financial statement?
posts.author: Ian Gow
posts.source_verification: Full articleBody and datePublished checked against public LinkedIn JSON-LD; also matches the previously captured authenticated feed text.
posts.original_post_text:
A prominent "get a job on Wall Street" guide asks: "What’s the most important financial statement?"

The provided answer: "The cash flow statement is the most important single statement because it tells you how much cash a company is generating. The income statement is misleading because it includes non-cash revenue and expenses and excludes cash spending such as capital expenditures."

Hmm. One approach to this answering this question might adapt the research design of Ball and Brown (1968). That paper essentially asked whether one would earn abnormal returns by having access to earnings news one year in advance. Answer: Yes.

The "get a job on Wall Street" guide might suggest we'd rather have information on the cash flow statement instead. But if you worked through the chapter in Empirical Research in Accounting on Ball and Brown (1968), you'd see that you'd do better with the income statement data (see exercise solutions in PDF below).

Empirical Research in Accounting: Tools and Methods
R version: https://lnkd.in/eP4jKiXH
Python version: https://lnkd.in/e2rQsRZn
posts.description: Using the Ball and Brown research design to examine the claim that the cash flow statement is the most important financial statement.

posts.title: Why include code in teaching?
posts.author: Ian Gow
posts.source_verification: Full articleBody and datePublished checked against public LinkedIn JSON-LD; also matches the previously captured authenticated feed text.
posts.original_post_text:
Including code in Empirical Research in Accounting: Tools and Methods had some downsides. For one, many instructors might feel uncomfortable with teaching material with code, especially if they are less familiar with the more modern languages (R and Python) used in the book. Another is the potential misperception that the book is *about* the code.

A good illustration of why including code makes sense is Chapter 21 ("Panel data"). While the book chapter explains the data sources and mechanics of the empirical analysis of the main paper, it's only in doing the exercises that students can really appreciate what's driving the paper's results (and how unconvincing these results seem to be when probed).

I include the solutions for that chapter in the PDF below.

Python version: https://lnkd.in/eH96gz3F
R version: https://lnkd.in/erHfTtQw
posts.description: Why working through code and exercises can reveal what drives a research paper's results, illustrated by the panel-data chapter.
